subject: chemistry
title: Key ideas
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Key ideas — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.11.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Key ideas, specification section 4.11.
final_note: You worked through Key ideas — 11 specification statements.

concepts.def: The tiny particle from which all matter is composed. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can still exist as that element.
A substance made of only one type of atom. There are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, and each type of atom is an element; the elements are set out in the periodic table.

A substance containing the atoms of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. Because about 100 elements can combine in an enormous number of ratios and arrangements, millions of different compounds exist.

The pattern by which similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals when the elements are arranged in order of atomic number. This repeating pattern is what the word 'periodic' in periodic table refers to.
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which is why they have similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied electron shells, and their properties change steadily across the row rather than staying similar.

The arrangement of the electrons in shells around the nucleus of an atom. It is this arrangement, and above all the number of electrons in the outer shell, that explains the periodic properties of the elements.

Bonding formed when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The oppositely charged ions produced are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction acting in all directions.
Bonding formed when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons. The shared pair is attracted to both nuclei at once, which is what holds the atoms together, and covalent bonds are strong.
An atom, or a group of atoms, that has lost or gained electrons and so carries an overall electrical charge. Losing electrons gives a positive ion; gaining electrons gives a negative ion.
A group of atoms bonded together by covalent bonds. The size and shape of a molecule, and the strength of the forces between one molecule and the next, affect how the substance behaves.

A structure in which very large numbers of atoms or ions are joined by a regular repeating network of strong bonds. Giant ionic lattices, giant covalent structures such as diamond and graphite, and metals are all giant structures.

The idea that the way the particles of a substance are arranged, and the strength of the forces holding them in place, decide its properties - its melting and boiling points, its hardness, and whether it conducts electricity.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react when they collide. It is the barrier to reaction: collisions with less than this energy do not lead to any chemical change.

How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Because different reactions have different energy barriers, and because conditions such as temperature, concentration and surface area differ, reactions occur at very different rates.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. A catalyst is not used up during the reaction.

A chemical change in which a hydrogen ion, H+, is passed from one substance to another. A hydrogen ion is a hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron, so it is a single proton; acid reactions with alkalis and bases work this way.
A chemical change in which electrons pass from one substance to another. Loss of electrons is oxidation and gain of electrons is reduction; the reaction of a metal with a non-metal works this way.
A chemical change in which atoms form covalent bonds by sharing pairs of electrons, rather than by giving electrons up or taking them. Reactions between non-metal elements work this way.

The principle that energy can be neither created nor destroyed. In a chemical reaction energy is only transferred, so the total amount of energy before the reaction equals the total amount afterwards.

An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature falls. In neither case is energy made or lost.

concepts.term: The three ways reactions take place
concepts.def: Chemical reactions take place in only three different ways: proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing. The many familiar names for reactions describe patterns, but underneath each is one of these three changes.

mcqs.q: Which statement about atoms and elements is correct?
options: Matter is made of tiny particles called atoms, and about 100 types occur naturally.
Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 different substances exist in total.
Matter is made of atoms, and every element shown in the periodic table occurs naturally.
Matter is made of atoms, and one type of atom exists for each known compound.
mcqs.explain: Matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms, and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, which are the elements.

mcqs.q: Millions of different compounds are known, yet there are only about 100 naturally occurring elements. How is this possible?
options: New types of atom are created every time a new compound is made.
Atoms of those elements combine in a huge variety of ratios and arrangements.
Most compounds contain elements that are not in the periodic table.
Compounds are only mixtures, so they are not limited by the elements.
mcqs.explain: A limited set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products, because atoms can join in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.

mcqs.q: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?
options: Every element in the same period of the table has very similar chemical properties.
All elements in one group behave identically, so their reactions look the same.
Similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals across the elements.
The properties of the elements change smoothly right across the whole table.
mcqs.explain: This is what 'periodic' means: arrange the elements in order of atomic number and similar properties come round again and again.

mcqs.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline solution. Which statement best explains this?
options: They are in the same period, so their chemical properties are bound to match.
They react at exactly the same rate, because group members are chemically the same.
They are metals, and every metal in the periodic table reacts with water like this.
They are in the same group, so they share a repeating pattern of chemical properties.
mcqs.explain: Group members have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why their chemical behaviour is alike.

mcqs.q: Why can the periodic properties of the elements be explained by atomic structure?
options: Because chemical properties depend on the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
Because chemical properties depend on the number of electrons in the outer shell.
Because chemical properties depend on the total number of electrons an atom contains.
Because chemical properties depend on how heavy the atom is compared to others.
mcqs.explain: Outer-shell electrons are the electrons involved in bonding, so the repeating pattern of outer-shell arrangements gives the repeating pattern of properties.

mcqs.q: Potassium reacts with water far more vigorously than lithium does. Which explanation is correct?
options: A potassium atom has more electrons in total, so it has more of them to give away.
A potassium atom has more outer-shell electrons than lithium, so it reacts faster.
Potassium has a larger relative atomic mass, and heavier atoms always react faster.
Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded, so it is lost easily.
mcqs.explain: Both metals lose one electron; greater distance and more shielding weaken the attraction on it, so it is lost more readily.

mcqs.q: According to this key idea, what are the two ways in which atoms bond together?
options: Electrons are shared between atoms, or protons are transferred between atoms.
Atoms are held by attraction between their nuclei, or by their opposite charges.
Electrons are transferred from one atom to another, or electrons are shared.
Electrons are transferred to fill outer shells, or the atoms simply stick together.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that atoms bond either by transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons.

mcqs.q: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. Which description of the bonding is correct?
options: Each magnesium atom shares two electrons with an oxygen atom, making two bonds.
Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg2+ and O2- ions.
Each magnesium atom gains two electrons from an oxygen atom, giving Mg2- ions.
Each magnesium atom transfers two protons to an oxygen atom, giving charged ions.
mcqs.explain: A metal reacting with a non-metal bonds by electron transfer; magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+ and oxygen gains them to form O2-.

mcqs.q: Chlorine boils at -34 degrees C, but silicon dioxide melts above 1600 degrees C. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The covalent bonds inside chlorine molecules are far weaker than those in silicon dioxide.
Silicon dioxide contains ionic bonds, and ionic bonding is always stronger than covalent.
Chlorine is a gas, and gases always have weaker bonds than solids at room temperature.
Chlorine exists as small molecules with weak forces between them; silicon dioxide is giant.
mcqs.explain: Boiling chlorine only overcomes weak forces between molecules, while melting silicon dioxide breaks strong covalent bonds throughout a giant structure.

mcqs.q: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, yet graphite is soft and conducts electricity. Why?
options: The covalent bonds in graphite are weak, so its atoms slide and its electrons move.
Graphite must contain a different element from diamond, which changes its properties.
The carbon atoms are arranged in layers with delocalised electrons between them.
Graphite is a metallic form of carbon, so free electrons let it conduct and bend.
mcqs.explain: Layers with no covalent bonds between them can slide, and the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge; the arrangement decides the behaviour.

mcqs.q: Ice melts at 0 degrees C but sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C. Which statement explains this difference?
options: Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of strongly attracted ions; ice is separate molecules.
The covalent bonds in water are weaker than the covalent bonds in sodium chloride.
Sodium chloride molecules are far larger and heavier than water molecules are.
Water is a liquid at room temperature, so its particles must be much further apart.
mcqs.explain: Melting the lattice must overcome strong electrostatic attraction between millions of ions, while melting ice only overcomes forces between molecules.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
options: The energy given out to the surroundings when particles collide successfully.
The energy that must be supplied by heating before an exothermic reaction starts.
The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
The total energy stored in the bonds of the reactants before the reaction begins.
mcqs.explain: Activation energy is the barrier to reaction: collisions carrying less than this energy produce no chemical change.

mcqs.q: Why does adding a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It gives the reacting particles extra energy, so more of them are able to react.
It provides a different reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy.
It increases the number of collisions by making the particles move much faster.
It is gradually used up in the reaction, which keeps the mixture warm throughout.
mcqs.explain: The barrier is lowered rather than the particles changed, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

mcqs.q: Why does raising the temperature have such a large effect on the rate of a reaction?
options: Heating lowers the activation energy, so the barrier becomes easier to cross.
A far greater proportion of collisions now have energy above the barrier.
Heating raises the concentration of the reactants, so more particles are present.
The particles collide more often, and that is the only reason the rate rises.
mcqs.explain: Higher temperature means more energetic particles, so many more collisions reach the activation energy; this outweighs the increase in collision frequency.

mcqs.q: The specification states that chemical reactions take place in only three different ways. What are they?
options: Proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing
Combustion, neutralisation and thermal decomposition
Proton transfer, neutron transfer and electron transfer
Oxidation, reduction and the neutralisation of an acid
mcqs.explain: These are the three ways the specification names immediately after the statement.

mcqs.q: Chemists give reactions many names, such as combustion, displacement and neutralisation. How does this fit with there being only three ways?
options: The names show that there are many more than three ways for reactions to happen.
Each named reaction involves all three of the changes happening one after another.
Only reactions given one of those three names count as reactions at GCSE level.
The names describe patterns, but the underlying change is always one of the three.
mcqs.explain: The names classify what a reaction looks like; the three ways classify what happens to the particles involved.

mcqs.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution. What is transferred in this reaction?
options: A whole hydrogen atom, complete with its electron, passes to the hydroxide ion.
A proton leaves the nucleus of a chlorine atom and joins the sodium nucleus.
A hydrogen ion, H+, which is a single proton, passes to the hydroxide ion.
An electron passes from the hydroxide ion to the acid, forming water and salt.
mcqs.explain: The acid supplies H+ ions, and each is a hydrogen atom stripped of its one electron, so it is a bare proton; H+ and OH- combine to form water.

mcqs.q: Which of these reactions is best described as proton transfer?
options: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide, giving sodium chloride and water
magnesium + oxygen, when a strip of magnesium burns brightly in air
zinc + copper sulfate solution, giving zinc sulfate and copper metal
hydrogen + chlorine, when the two gases combine to form hydrogen chloride
mcqs.explain: An acid reacting with an alkali passes H+ ions to OH- ions, which is proton transfer.

mcqs.q: In terms of electrons, what happens during oxidation and reduction?
options: Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction is the loss of electrons.
Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.
Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction is the gain of protons.
Oxidation is the gain of oxygen only, and electrons are not involved at all.
mcqs.explain: This is the electron definition, summarised as OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

mcqs.q: Sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl2 gives 2NaCl. Which statement about the electrons is correct?
options: Each sodium atom loses one electron and each chlorine atom gains one electron.
Each sodium atom gains one electron and each chlorine atom loses one electron.
Each sodium atom shares one electron with a chlorine atom, forming a bond.
Each sodium atom loses two electrons, which both chlorine atoms then share.
mcqs.explain: Sodium is oxidised to Na+ and chlorine is reduced to Cl-, so the reaction proceeds by electron transfer.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3. How does this reaction take place?
options: By electron transfer: nitrogen takes electrons from hydrogen, giving ions.
By proton transfer: hydrogen atoms give their protons to nitrogen atoms.
By electron sharing: nitrogen and hydrogen atoms share pairs of electrons.
By neither: the molecules stick together with no bonds broken or made.
mcqs.explain: Both elements are non-metals, so they bond by sharing electrons to form covalent bonds in the ammonia molecule.

mcqs.q: What does the conservation of energy mean for a chemical reaction?
options: Energy is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings, never made.
Energy is created by exothermic reactions and destroyed by endothermic ones.
The temperature of the surroundings cannot change, since energy is conserved.
Energy is used up as the reaction proceeds, so less exists at the end.
mcqs.explain: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions and can be neither created nor destroyed; a reaction only moves it.

mcqs.q: Citric acid solution is added to sodium hydrogencarbonate and the temperature of the mixture falls. What has happened to the energy?
options: Energy has been destroyed by the reaction, which is why the temperature drops.
Energy has been created inside the solution but cannot be felt as warmth.
The energy of the surroundings is unchanged and the thermometer is misreading.
Energy has been taken in from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool.
mcqs.explain: This is an endothermic reaction: energy moves from the surroundings into the chemicals, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
